newsitem.title: UK: British MPs urge tighter net on Russian espionage.
newsitem.headline: British MPs urge tighter net on Russian espionage.

text.p: Britain's intelligence services were urged on Monday to improve their defences against possible Russian infiltration in light of the damage done to the United States by Central Intelligence Agency traitor Aldrich Ames.

Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee, made up of senior legislators, said in its annual report that British interests did not seem to have been seriously harmed by Ames, whose spying for Russia led to the death of several CIA agents.

But the panel said the affair, and the arrest last year of another CIA, Harold Nicholson, on charges of spying for Moscow, was a powerful reminder of the continuing threat from the Russians and others.

"It is critically important to be sure that our defences are fully effective against all these threats. On the evidence we have taken, we believe that there are a number of areas where our defences are not as strong as they should be," it said.
Ames was finally caught after his lavish lifestyle, and the expensive tastes of his second wife, raised suspicions, the committee's chairman, Conservative MP Tom King, told reporters.
He disclosed that all of Britain's three main spy agencies had refused or withdrawn security clearance in recent years from contractors and staff members who had run up big debts.
"Signs that individuals are greatly overspending their income, without any visible external means, should be of similar concern," the report by King's committee said.
"The particular relevance of this is that money, rather than ideology, is the principal motivation of an increasing number of agents," it added.
Among precautions it recommended are the investigation of individuals' finances, frequent vetting reviews and random searches of staff entering and leaving secure buildings.

King, a former defence minister, stressed that there was no evidence of an Ames at work in Britain's intelligence services -- the MI5 security service, the MI6 overseas intelligence service and the GCHQ electronic eavesdropping installation at Cheltenham in western England.
But, equally, he said there was no reason to suppose that Moscow was not trying to infiltrate them.
"Russians are still the top threat," he said.

Intelligence experts are particularly worried that there is nothing to stop a disgruntled employee from revealing top secret information purely out of spite, for example by publishing it on the Internet, according to members of the committee.
The report said it had considered what steps the intelligence services could take to counter this threat and said it was vital that they draw up contingency plans for a worst-case scenario.

"It is also important for ministers to be aware of the range of options that might be considered. We have not yet had a chance to establish how well equipped each agency is in this respect," the committee said.

On other issues, the panel disclosed that MI5 had considerably increased the resources devoted to countering the Irish Republican Army after the guerrilla group resumed its attacks against British targets a year ago.

It commended MI5, in its campaign against the IRA, on "some significant successes based on painstaking intelligence work" and said the intelligence and security services overall gave good service to Britain.
